headline: AI Prompts Can Leak Secrets Like Pastebin, Dev Warns
summary: Pasting sensitive data into AI prompts is the new way to leak secrets, with no way to delete them later. A developer explains the risks and how to avoid them.
details: Developers are increasingly using AI tools to help write code, but a new warning highlights a significant security risk: accidentally pasting sensitive information like database credentials into prompts.

This data can end up in AI provider logs or even training sets, creating a permanent leak that cannot be deleted. The author likens this to the old practice of pasting secrets into Pastebin, but with less control.

The article stresses that AI providers are 'trusted but unverified third parties.' While paid tiers offer stronger privacy guarantees like no-training agreements, they still retain request logs and may have other sub-processors or retention policies.

The recommended approach is not to avoid AI, but to treat AI prompts as untrusted egress, similar to any outbound network call from production. This means masking sensitive data with placeholders like [API_KEY] or [DB_PASSWORD].

Using placeholders allows AI models to reason effectively without exposing actual secrets. This practice helps prevent data exfiltration, especially for developers already dealing with secrets sprawl.

For highly sensitive data like payment or health information, using consumer-grade AI tiers is strongly discouraged. Local or self-hosted models are recommended only when data is regulated and must never transit a third party.

The core principle is defense in depth: even with a 'no-training' guarantee, treat the prompt channel with a zero-trust posture. This involves verifying, scoping, and minimizing the context sent to the AI, ensuring the cheapest secret to protect is the one that never leaves the machine.

headline_marked: [[Buddy System]] routes LLM inference with Rust entropy monitor
headline: Buddy System routes LLM inference with Rust entropy monitor
summary: A new architecture uses a Rust entropy monitor to intelligently route LLM queries between local models and cloud APIs, optimizing performance and cost.
details: Frontier LLM inference is expensive. A developer built a tiered inference architecture called Buddy System, using a Rust entropy monitor to track per-token uncertainty during local generation. This system routes queries to cloud APIs like Sonnet only when the local model is genuinely stuck, aiming to optimize performance and cost.

The system leverages Gemma 3 4B running locally on Apple Silicon via MLX. A Rust EntropyMonitor, compiled as a PyO3 extension, computes Shannon entropy over the full token vocabulary for every generated token. At high-entropy clause boundaries (threshold: 0.8), spaCy NER identifies specific entities or noun chunks the model is uncertain about.

A sentence-transformers retriever finds relevant passage chunks. Sonnet then receives a targeted query, including the uncertain fact and the grounding document. Crucially, all cloud calls are asynchronous and fire after local generation completes, ensuring the generation process itself is never blocked by API latency.

Buddy System also incorporates classical tools for deterministic answers, such as math, dates, and units, handling these at zero cost between local and cloud tiers. This contrasts with simpler advisor patterns where cloud models correct from parametric memory without access to the original source document.

The article highlights that passing the document to the reviewer tier significantly improves results, as demonstrated by the Buddy System's retrieval step. This approach led to a 30pp improvement on SQuAD v2 and a 20pp improvement on HotpotQA compared to local-only generation, suggesting a more effective use of cloud AI resources.
